title: Composite Factorial Vanishing: n divides (n-1)!
content: For composite n > 4, n divides (n-1)!. The proof splits into two cases: (1) n = p² for an odd prime p ≥ 3: then 2p ≤ n-1, and p, 2p are distinct factors in (n-1)!, so p·2p = 2p² divides (n-1)! — and p² divides 2p², giving p² | (n-1)!. (2) n = p·q with p ≠ q: both p and q appear in {1,...,n-1}, and distinct_factors_dvd_factorial gives p·q | (n-1)!. The key infrastructure is distinct_factors_dvd_factorial, which uses Finset.prod_dvd_prod_of_subset.
mathContext:
\text{Composite } n > 4 \Rightarrow n \mid (n-1)!\\
\text{Case 1: } n = p^2\ (p \geq 3) \Rightarrow p \cdot 2p = 2p^2 \mid (n-1)!,\; p^2 \mid 2p^2 \Rightarrow n \mid (n-1)!\\
\text{Case 2: } n = pq,\ p \neq q \Rightarrow p,q \in \{1,\ldots,n-1\},\; pq \mid (n-1)!

title: Wilson's Complete Trichotomy for All n≥2
content: wilson_complete_classification establishes the exact trichotomy of (n-1)! mod n for all n ≥ 2: (1) n prime → (n-1)! ≡ -1 (mod n) by Wilson's theorem; (2) n = 4 → (n-1)! = 3! = 6 ≡ 2 (mod 4), the unique exception; (3) n composite, n > 4 → (n-1)! ≡ 0 (mod n) by composite_factorial_dvd. The case n = 4 is the only composite where (n-1)! mod n is neither 0 nor -1. prime_iff_factorial_neg_one then gives the biconditional: n is prime iff (n-1)! ≡ -1 (mod n), a primality test via Mathlib's Nat.prime_iff_fac_equiv_neg_one.
mathContext:
\forall n \geq 2:\; (n-1)! \equiv \begin{cases} -1 \pmod{n} & n \text{ prime} \\ 2 \pmod{4} & n = 4 \\ 0 \pmod{n} & n \text{ composite},\ n > 4 \end{cases}\\
n \text{ prime} \iff (n-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{n}

title: Wilson Quotient: Integer Quotient of (p-1)!+1 by p
content: For any prime p, Wilson's theorem guarantees p | (p-1)!+1. The Wilson quotient W_p = ((p-1)!+1)/p is always an integer (wilsonQuotient_mul) and always positive (wilsonQuotient_pos). Concrete values: W_2=1, W_3=1, W_5=5, W_7=103, W_11=329891, W_13=36846277. A prime p is a Wilson prime iff p | W_p (i.e., p² | (p-1)!+1). The quotient grows super-exponentially: W_p ≈ (p-1)!/p.
mathContext:
W_p = \frac{(p-1)! + 1}{p} \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}\\
p \text{ Wilson prime} \iff p \mid W_p \iff p^2 \mid (p-1)!+1\\
W_5 = 5,\; W_7 = 103,\; W_{13} = 36846277

title: Wilson Primes: p² divides (p-1)!+1
content: IsWilsonPrime p asserts p is prime and p² | (p-1)!+1 — a second-order divisibility condition. While every prime p divides (p-1)!+1, a Wilson prime requires the square p² to divide it. Verified: five_is_wilson_prime (4!+1=25=5²) and thirteen_is_wilson_prime (12!+1 divisible by 169). Non-Wilson primes proved: 2, 3, 7, 11. The only known Wilson primes are 5, 13, and 563. Connection to Bernoulli numbers: p is Wilson prime iff p | B_{p-1}.
mathContext:
\text{IsWilsonPrime}(p) \iff p \text{ prime} \wedge p^2 \mid (p-1)!+1\\
4! + 1 = 25 = 5^2 \Rightarrow 5 \text{ is Wilson prime}\\
12! + 1 = 479001601 \equiv 0 \pmod{169} \Rightarrow 13 \text{ is Wilson prime}\\
p \text{ Wilson prime} \iff p \mid B_{p-1}

title: Units Product and Gauss-Wilson Form Check
content: unitsProduct n = ∏{a < n : gcd(a,n)=1} a is the product of all units mod n. hasGaussWilsonForm n decidably checks whether n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k} for odd prime p, using isPowerOfAux. gaussWilsonCheck verifies that unitsProduct n % n = n-1 iff hasGaussWilsonForm n. Computationally confirmed via native_decide for all n ≤ 50 (gaussWilson_verified_le_50) and extended to n ≤ 200 (gaussWilson_verified_le_200). This gives empirical confidence before the abstract algebraic proof.
mathContext:
\text{unitsProduct}(n) = \prod_{\substack{a < n \\ \gcd(a,n)=1}} a\\
\text{GaussWilsonForm} \iff n \in \{1,2,4,p^k,2p^k\} \text{ for odd prime } p\\
\forall n \leq 200:\; \text{unitsProduct}(n) \bmod n = n-1 \iff \text{GaussWilsonForm}(n)

title: Square Roots of Unity: Key to Gauss-Wilson Product Formula
content: sqRootsOfUnity n = {a : gcd(a,n)=1, a²≡1 (mod n)} are the self-inverse units. The key structural insight: non-self-inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹) cancel in ∏units, leaving ∏units ≡ ∏{self-inverse units}. For Gauss-Wilson forms: exactly 2 square roots of unity — {1, n-1} — so product = n-1 ≡ -1. For other n: ≥ 4 square roots forming a (ℤ/2)^k subgroup with product 1. This explains why Gauss-Wilson forms give -1 and others give 1. Computationally verified for n ≤ 100 (sqRoot_gaussWilson_le_100).

title: Abstract Gauss-Wilson: IsCyclic Characterization via Mathlib
content: isCyclic_units_iff_gaussWilson restates Mathlib's ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff in simplified form for n ≥ 3: (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic iff n = 4 or ∃ p odd prime, k ≥ 1 with n = p^k or n = 2p^k. The proof is a pure case analysis over Mathlib's output, filtering the n = 0,1,2 cases and mapping Odd p ↔ p ≠ 2. This is the abstract group-theoretic heart: cyclic unit group ↔ primitive root exists ↔ Gauss-Wilson holds.

title: Gauss-Wilson Classification: The Main Theorem
content: gaussWilson_classification is the culminating theorem: for n ≥ 3, unitsProduct n % n = n-1 iff n ∈ {4, p^k, 2p^k} for odd prime p. The proof chain: (1) unitsProduct_eq_neg_one_iff_cyclic reduces the concrete arithmetic to IsCyclic (ℤ/nℤ)* via WilsonsTheoremOQ02's abstract bridge; (2) isCyclic_units_iff_gaussWilson (restating Mathlib's ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff) gives the p^k/2p^k characterization. This connects 200-case computational verification with the abstract group-theoretic proof.
mathContext:
\prod_{\gcd(a,n)=1} a \equiv -1 \pmod{n} \iff n = 4 \vee \exists p \text{ odd prime},\ k \geq 1:\; n = p^k \vee n = 2p^k\\
\text{Proof: concrete} \xrightarrow{\text{bridge (OQ02)}} \text{IsCyclic} \xrightarrow{\text{Mathlib}} p^k/2p^k
